lessons.title: Frequency, dB and distortion
lessons.description: Start here: musical frequencies, decibels, clean sound, and how to read a speaker-response curve.
lessons.next_bridge: Now that frequency, loudness and distortion make sense, see how a speaker's response curve helps explain the sound of familiar music.

lessons.title: Speaker frequency response
lessons.description: Understand why speakers sound balanced, bright, warm or forward.
lessons.next_bridge: Once you can read a frequency-response graph, follow the curve into the lowest notes to understand what bass extension actually describes.

lessons.title: Bass extension
lessons.description: See how the deepest bass notes fade and why the shape matters.
lessons.next_bridge: Deep bass alone doesn't tell you how loudly a speaker can play. Sensitivity connects its output to the power going in.

lessons.title: Speaker sensitivity
lessons.description: Learn why some speakers play louder from the same amplifier input.
lessons.next_bridge: Sensitivity tells you how much sound you get for a given input. Impedance tells you what electrical load the amplifier has to drive.

lessons.title: Speaker impedance and matching
lessons.description: Read speaker impedance curves, nominal ohms, and amplifier load requirements.
lessons.question: Why doesn't an 8-ohm speaker stay at 8 ohms?
lessons.decode: The 8 Ω figure is a nominal designation, not a constant value. A minimum of 6.4 Ω means the magnitude is stated not to fall below 80% of nominal in the rated band. That relationship appears in IEC 60268-5. A typical impedance plot may rise dramatically at a driver's resonance without implying louder sound at those frequencies.
lessons.limit: The rating tells you neither the phase angle nor how much current your specific amplifier can safely deliver. This fictional curve illustrates the specification, not a tested speaker.
heads: A deep dip can challenge an amplifier
exps: The magnitude rises around the bass resonance and comes back down. An ordinary speaker does not have one perfectly fixed impedance across all music.
A typical 4 Ω nominal loudspeaker runs at a lower electrical impedance. It can be every bit as good as an 8 Ω design, but a compatible amplifier must supply the current.
A substantial dip may increase current demand at particular frequencies, especially with an unfavorable electrical phase. This is something to investigate, not automatic evidence of bad sound.
paragraphs: Impedance measures opposition to alternating electrical current. A speaker has moving voice coils, crossover components and resonances, so its impedance changes with the frequency of the signal. The single number on the carton is shorthand for the load an amplifier should expect.

A low impedance at a given output voltage generally asks the amplifier for more current. A high resonant peak, by contrast, does not automatically increase amplifier load. Even more important, a magnitude curve doesn't show electrical phase, which changes how current and voltage interact.

When two different speakers are equally loud and their amplifiers are operating comfortably, the nominal 4 Ω or 8 Ω labels do not define the sound. The meaningful risk is exceeding a particular amplifier's stable operating range.
listening: An amplifier may sound clean with a demanding loudspeaker at modest levels, then approach clipping, protection or excess heating when a loud passage requires more current. That is a system interaction, not proof that low impedance inherently sounds worse.

Bass tightness, separation and musical dynamics cannot be read directly from nominal impedance. Speaker response, sensitivity, distortion, placement and the amplifier's actual capabilities all play roles.
lessons.audiophile: “Eight-ohm speakers are easy to drive” and “four-ohm speakers have more powerful bass” are common shortcuts. A nominal label alone doesn't establish either conclusion.
lessons.evidence: Impedance magnitude and phase, minimum impedance, listening level and amplifier current/voltage capacity all influence matching. A nominal 8 Ω speaker can still present surprisingly challenging dips. IEC 60268-5 includes a rated-impedance minimum-magnitude convention.
buy: Check the rated load supported by the amplifier, and look for minimum impedance rather than only nominal impedance.
Consider sensitivity and listening distance: a nominal rating doesn't tell you how loudly the speaker will play for a given input.
Avoid connecting multiple speakers in parallel without understanding how their combined load affects the amplifier.
lessons.advanced: For a pure resistor only, I = V/R. At 20 V RMS, 8 Ω draws 2.5 A and 4 Ω draws 5 A. Loudspeakers are complex frequency-dependent loads, so the instantaneous relationship also depends on phase.
sources: Loudspeaker impedance and IEC standard examples
lessons.next_bridge: With the electrical load understood, look inside the cabinet at the drivers and crossover that turn the signal into sound.

lessons.title: Speaker drivers, materials and crossovers
lessons.description: Understand woofers, tweeters, cone materials, surrounds and the crossover between them.
lessons.next_bridge: Driver design matters, but so does where that sound travels. Next, explore what changes when you move away from the centre seat.

lessons.title: Speaker dispersion and off-axis response
lessons.description: Why sound changes away from the centre seat, how to read horizontal/vertical response and speaker directivity.
lessons.next_bridge: Now that coverage and listening position make sense, compare the speaker designs used at desks, in living rooms, in studios and for audiences.

lessons.title: Speaker types: hi-fi, studio, nearfield and PA
lessons.description: Understand which loudspeaker designs suit a desk, living room, stage or audience, and where their uses overlap.
lessons.next_bridge: You've followed the speaker side of the system. Next, see how much clean amplifier power it takes to play music at the level you want.

lessons.title: Amplifier power
lessons.description: Understand clean output, headroom and meaningful wattage ratings.
lessons.next_bridge: Watts describe rated output, but not everything that happens as an amplifier works harder. Next, learn what distortion measurements reveal.

lessons.title: Amplifier distortion and harmonics
lessons.description: Compare distortion curves and understand the added tones.
lessons.next_bridge: Now that distortion graphs have meaning, look at amplifier designs without mistaking a circuit-class label for a sound-quality ranking.

lessons.title: Amplifier classes and devices
lessons.description: Compare Class A, AB, D and G/H, and distinguish operating classes from device types.
lessons.question: Does Class A, Class AB or Class D decide how an amplifier sounds?
lessons.decode: Class AB describes the operating method: complementary output devices share the audio signal with some overlap. MOSFET describes the kind of transistor used. Both terms can describe one amplifier, because operating class and transistor type are independent design choices.
lessons.limit: The label doesn't reveal the amplifier's wattage, distortion, output impedance or noise. It isn't enough to predict whether the amplifier will sound warm, clinical or transparent.
exps: Class A keeps its output devices conducting across the waveform cycle. It can avoid some crossover mechanisms, but usually expends significant power as heat, even at idle.
Class AB shares the waveform across devices with overlap to reduce crossover distortion. Its mix of efficiency and performance makes it common in hi-fi and home-theater equipment.
Class D uses devices as rapid switches, typically followed by an output filter. It can be extremely efficient and accurate. The D does not stand for digital audio.
paragraphs: Operating class describes how the amplifier's output stage handles the signal. In conventional linear stages, Class A conducts throughout the cycle; Class B splits the cycle; Class AB overlaps the split to reduce crossover distortion. Class D uses high-speed switching instead.

The hardware uses specific devices. Vacuum tubes, bipolar junction transistors (BJTs) and MOSFETs describe what controls electrical current, not the amplifier class. A Class AB amplifier may use MOSFETs or BJTs. Tubes can also be used in Class A or AB designs.

Classes G and H manage the supply-rail voltages to reduce waste. They may be combined with linear output stages. Practical concerns such as cooling, reliability, output limits and power consumption often differ by design.
listening: A carefully engineered Class D amplifier can reproduce music very accurately, just as a well-made Class AB amplifier can. The class label alone does not prove that one will have smoother guitars or punchier drums.

Some tube designs or other deliberately colored circuits can add audible harmonics. That coloration depends on the particular circuitry and load, not merely the presence of tubes, MOSFETs or a Class A badge.
lessons.audiophile: “Class A is the most musical,” “MOSFETs sound like tubes” and “Class D sounds cold” are useful claims to investigate, not universal laws. Different implementations can measure and sound very different.
lessons.evidence: Amplifier operating class is strongly related to heat, efficiency and design requirements. A class label by itself cannot establish a distortion spectrum or a reliably audible tonal character.
buy: Compare clean power, THD+N at relevant loads and levels, and compatibility with the speakers you actually own.
Account for idle heat, ventilation and service needs; tube replacement and Class A power consumption can add ongoing costs.
Read actual product measurements rather than relying on the output-device label as a substitute for sound-quality evidence.
lessons.advanced: In a conventional linear output stage, a Class A device conducts for 360° of the cycle; Class B approximately 180°; Class AB between 180° and 360°. Class D uses switching rather than the same conduction-angle classification. Class G/H implement different supply-rail management strategies.
sources: Analog Devices: Class D amplifier design and efficiency
lessons.next_bridge: Speakers and amplifiers are one way to listen. Headphones bring the sound closer to your ears, making their construction and fit especially important.

lessons.title: Headphones and IEM types
lessons.description: Compare three earcup enclosures and see how over-ear, on-ear, earbud and IEM fits differ.
lessons.next_bridge: Knowing how headphones are built makes their frequency-response curves easier to understand, especially when pads or ear tips change the seal.

lessons.title: Headphone frequency response and fit
lessons.description: Read a 20 Hz–20 kHz rating and see how tuning and a pad leak change the bass.
lessons.next_bridge: A tonal-balance curve does not tell you how demanding headphones are to drive. Next, connect sensitivity and impedance to volts and power.

lessons.title: Headphone sensitivity and impedance
lessons.description: Compare dB SPL per volt and per milliwatt, then work out the voltage and current needed.
lessons.next_bridge: You can now estimate what the headphones need. Next, see how the headphone output itself can change the sound or available level.

lessons.title: Headphone output impedance and source matching
lessons.description: See how a headphone jack and a changing load divide voltage and can alter tonal balance.
lessons.next_bridge: You've followed the headphone connection. Now trace the sources that send music to headphones, amplifiers and speakers.

lessons.title: Playback sources: vinyl, CD, DACs and sound cards
lessons.description: Follow music from vinyl, CDs, computers and streamers to the amplifier, with RIAA and connection examples.
lessons.next_bridge: Once the source connections are clear, look at signal levels to understand what happens when a player or DAC connects to an amplifier.

lessons.title: Source levels and amplifier input sensitivity
lessons.description: Why a 2 V source does not automatically overload an input rated at 200 mV sensitivity.
lessons.next_bridge: With source levels explained, noise, distortion and output specifications for a DAC become much easier to interpret.

lessons.title: DAC noise, output level and distortion
lessons.description: Learn to read SNR, THD+N, voltage levels and the limits of DAC specifications.
lessons.next_bridge: A DAC is one part of the signal path. Next, discover how microphones, mixers and computer interfaces bring sounds into a recording.

lessons.title: Audio interfaces, mixers and recording channels
lessons.description: See what a microphone preamp, computer audio interface and mixer each do, and why mixer channels are not necessarily separate recorded tracks.
lessons.next_bridge: Now that inputs, mixer channels and recorded tracks are clear, look at how digital audio stores the changing signal over time.

lessons.title: Sample rates and audio bandwidth
lessons.description: Decode 48,000 samples per second, Nyquist bandwidth, aliasing and sample-rate choices.
lessons.next_bridge: Sample rate describes how often the signal is represented. Bit depth describes the resolution of each stored sample.

lessons.title: Bit depth and dynamic range
lessons.description: Understand 16-bit versus 24-bit PCM, quantization, noise and dither without confusing bits with musical dynamics.
lessons.next_bridge: With sample rate and bit depth understood, see how lossless and lossy formats handle that digital audio information.

lessons.title: Lossless vs lossy audio and bitrates
lessons.description: Understand MP3, AAC, FLAC, PCM, bitrate and the artifacts a codec might create.
lessons.next_bridge: You've followed the music file to the listener. Now follow the signal back to the performances, microphones and instruments that created the recording.

lessons.title: Microphones, DI and virtual instruments
lessons.description: Trace microphones, direct instrument inputs, hardware synths and software instruments into a recording; see how mic placement and a room change the captured sound.
lessons.next_bridge: Once you've decided what to record, microphone design and placement help determine what actually gets captured.

lessons.title: Microphone types and practical uses
lessons.description: Compare dynamic, condenser, ribbon, shotgun and other microphones by how they work and the jobs they suit.
lessons.next_bridge: After the sound reaches an input, learn to set recording gain and preserve the signal cleanly before mixing.

lessons.title: Recording resolution, gain and oversampling
lessons.description: Explore 24-bit recording headroom, real clipping limits, 32-bit float and how oversampling prevents a particular digital alias.
lessons.next_bridge: With the tracks captured, see how mixing balances instruments and creates the impression of space, distance and separation.

lessons.title: Mixing, soundstage and spatial audio
lessons.description: Watch pan, EQ, ambience and mic timing alter a fictional mix; understand binaural recording, QSound, 5.1, Atmos and the listener's soundstage.
lessons.next_bridge: Once the mix takes shape, mastering prepares it for release. Next, compare how different masters change loudness, tone and dynamics.

lessons.title: Mastering, remastering and dynamic range
lessons.description: Compare three masters of the same performance, learn why editions sound different, and see how matching peaks or average level changes what the amp has to deliver.
lessons.next_bridge: You've followed the signal from sound waves and equipment through recording, mixing and mastering. Use the lessons as a reference whenever you need them.

fundamentals.label: Basics
fundamentals.description: Understand pitch, level and distortion before decoding equipment specifications.

speakers.label: Speakers
speakers.description: Explore how speakers turn an electrical signal into sound, from tonal balance to bass and sensitivity.

amplifiers.label: Amplifiers
amplifiers.description: Discover what amplifier power, distortion and circuit performance mean when driving real speakers.

headphones.label: Headphones & IEMs
headphones.description: Explore earcup design, fit, frequency response and how headphones interact with the source.

sources.label: Sources & DACs
sources.description: Follow vinyl, CD, sound cards, streaming and DACs into the amplifier, then decode levels and audio formats.

recording.label: Recording & Production
recording.description: Follow the recording from microphones, DI and virtual instruments through mixing, mastering and playback.
